groups.name: TV shows whose title doubles as an emotional self-description of its protagonist
groups.explanation: Fleabag (a mess of a person), Enlightened (Amy's delusion of spiritual awakening), I'm Sorry (Andrea Savage's constant mortified apologising), and Hacks (Deborah Vance's self-aware label as a comedian past her prime) are all dramedy show titles that function as a blunt emotional or social self-assessment pinned directly to the lead character.

groups.name: TV characters whose storyline centrally involves an unwanted teenage pregnancy
groups.explanation: Debbie Gallagher (Shameless US) becomes pregnant at 15; Becca Brady (The Secret Life of the American Teenager) is the central unwanted teen pregnancy figure; Amy Jellicoe — TRAP: Amy Jellicoe is from Enlightened, not a teen pregnancy show, prompting second-guessing. Replacing: Kat Edison (The Bold Type) supports a storyline involving an unplanned pregnancy among her circle. More precisely: Debbie Gallagher (Shameless US — teen pregnancy arc), Becca (The Secret Life of the American Teenager — central premise), Paige Michalchuk (Degrassi — abortion/unwanted pregnancy arc), and Stella (Misfits — teen pregnancy). Revised tiles used: Debbie Gallagher (Shameless US), Becca Brady (Secret Life), Paige Michalchuk (Degrassi: The Next Generation), and Stella (Misfits UK). Adjusting tile_7 to Paige Michalchuk and tile_8 to Stella.

groups.name: Women who created and starred in their own semi-autobiographical TV comedy
groups.explanation: Phoebe Waller-Bridge created and starred in Fleabag; Michaela Coel created and starred in I May Destroy You; Lena Dunham created and starred in Girls; Mindy Kaling created and starred in The Mindy Project. All four are women who drew heavily from their own lives to build their shows and played the lead. TRAP: Phoebe Waller-Bridge also appears indirectly via tile_1 (Fleabag the show title), tempting solvers to link her there instead.

groups.name: Iconic fictional TV women from the 1990s–2000s who never married the fathers of their children
groups.explanation: Murphy Brown (Murphy Brown) famously had her son Avery as a single mother, sparking a national debate; Liz Lemon (30 Rock) ultimately adopts as a single woman before marrying Criss — but her iconic identity is the career-obsessed woman who never had a conventional family; Dana Scully (The X-Files) had William under ambiguous paternity circumstances and gave him up without marrying Mulder; C.J. Cregg (The West Wing) never married and had no children in the series. This group needs a cleaner, verifiable thread. Revised concept: Iconic fictional TV career women of the 1990s–2000s defined by their professional identity over romantic fulfilment — Murphy Brown (journalist), Liz Lemon (TV producer), Dana Scully (FBI agent/scientist), C.J. Cregg (White House Press Secretary). All four are widely cited as groundbreaking portrayals of ambitious professional women on American TV whose careers were the engine of their shows.
